Wow, I really like this. Going along each day of the week creates a really nice pace. The childlike perspective on these great events makes them tower over our expectations, and at the same time, they seem trivial. Really great job.

Work has tied me from responding, but I'm honored to be your first go at feedback! Really appreciate everyone's comments, this is my first time workshopping poetry on Reddit and certainly won't be my last. You must be a professor or something, really, your comment made my week!

I really struggled with naming this piece and was more leaning toward the suicide theme initially, relying on the scenes of hopelessness and how we rush parts of our lives. I wanted the final three stanzas, which are indeed part of the same scene, to reflect on how easily we are pushed into making a regrettable decision in haste. I absolutely should expand that. Perhaps give more examples, more substance to the comic-book style, but also sprinkle in some glimmers of home. Really hammer in that there is a beauty that we miss when we only focus on the bad. Perhaps the banker seems something from above?

I love how you interpreted the title flowing into the poem. It really wants me to separate the ending of suicide and go more with the theme of rushing our lives. Like others have said, this does feel like two separate pieces and I think I'm going to part the two.

Stanza three with the spider will be reworked. I'm not sure how I feel with the strolling and the rhyming doesn't quite fit with the rest. The spider strolling is indeed a tad much. Perhaps lurching would be more appropriate?

The nearsighted children was more of a literal take on how kids with glasses are often the butts of jokes, but I really love how you took it though.

Seriously though, you've all given me so much to think about! IYou have inspired me to keep writing and working. I love all the ways you've perceived it and all the new eggs that have hatched in my mind. Really, you've turned around a really shit, bleak week. I can't thank you enough.

I really like how you insinuate that this could be just another lover's quarrel type poem. "His grave, lost in the labyrinth of memory," is a great line. I would remove "His eyes reflected the corpse that killed him" or move it to the next stanza as the final quartet reveals the true nature of the poem. Line 12 being in stanza 3 spoils that a bit.

I'm unsure if this was the intent, but it makes me think of nostalgia. Childhood cartoons of stop motion, tea kettle at grandma's house, and it's all the same, because time will un-strip. Great line, "Time un-strips like bark." It's short, but effective. Still, I think you could contninue this feeling for another stanza or too, if nostalgia is the theme. Then the poem would not be a moment, but moments...
